function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

**Reykjavík – the clear winner for an ice‑hockey‑focused trip** | Why Reykjavík stands out | Practical tips | |---------------------------|----------------| | **Largest and most modern rink** – *Reykjavík Ice Rink* (Hraunshól) is the only full‑size, regulation‑size arena in Iceland. It hosts the national team, the Icelandic Hockey League (Íshokkísamband Íslands), and the annual Icelandic Hockey Cup. | • **Location** – in the heart of the capital, easily reachable by bus, taxi, or rental car.
• **Accommodation** – a wide range of hotels, hostels, and Airbnbs from budget to luxury. | | **National team & league action** – Reykjavík is home to the Icelandic national team’s training camps and the league’s regular season and playoffs. If you time your visit right, you can catch a live game, meet players, and even attend a practice session. | • **Tickets** – buy online via the Icelandic Hockey Association’s website or at the rink’s box office.
• **Schedule** – check the league calendar (usually late spring to early autumn) and the national team’s fixtures. | | **Ice‑hockey culture** – The city hosts the annual *Icelandic Hockey Festival*, featuring youth clinics, exhibition matches, and community events. It’s a great way to see the sport’s grassroots side. | • **Events** – look for the *Icelandic Hockey Festival* (usually in July) and the *Icelandic Hockey Cup* finals (late summer). | | **Convenient travel hub** – Keflavík International Airport is just 20 km away, and the city’s public transport network makes getting around easy. | • **Transport** – use the “Raxi” bus service or the free “Reykjavík City Bus” for short trips. | | **Other attractions** – While you’re in Reykjavík, you can combine your hockey trip with Iceland’s iconic sights: the Hallgrímskirkja church, Harpa concert hall, the Blue Lagoon, and the Golden Circle. | • **Dining** – try local Icelandic cuisine at restaurants like *Matur og Drykkur* or *Kaffi Loki*. | --- ### Quick comparison with other Icelandic cities | City | Ice‑hockey facilities | Notes | |------|-----------------------|-------| | **Reykjavík** | 1 full‑size rink, national team, league games | Best overall for hockey fans | | **Akureyri** | 1 smaller rink, hosts some league games | Good secondary option, quieter | | **Húsavík / Ísafjörður** | Small rinks, occasional friendly matches | Limited professional activity | --- ### How to plan your visit 1. **Check the league calendar** – The Icelandic Hockey League runs from late May to early September. The playoffs and finals are usually in August–September. 2. **Book tickets in advance** – Popular games (e.g., national team matches) sell out quickly. 3. **Arrange accommodation early** – Reykjavík’s hotels fill up during the summer months. 4. **Combine with other Icelandic experiences** – Use Reykjavík as a base to explore nearby attractions or take day trips to the Golden Circle, Blue Lagoon, or the Westfjords. --- **Bottom line:** If you’re looking for the richest ice‑hockey experience in Iceland, Reykjavík is the place to be. It offers the best facilities, the most competitive games, and the convenience of a major city. Akureyri is a solid backup if you prefer a quieter setting, but Reykjavík remains the top choice for any hockey enthusiast.
